docs.title: What Survives
docs.text:
When voters pass a law by ballot initiative, the legislature can often amend or repeal it. Current records label a technical fix and a gutting the same way: altered. This project measures what actually survives, provision by provision, and publishes the evidence so anyone can check it.

The claim in one sentence: existing methods measure whether the text changed; this measures whether the law still does what voters voted for.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Phase Prototype Cases coded (first pass) 1 of ~15 planned for hand verification Schema version 0.2 (see changelog) Pipeline Designed, not built Hand-verified gold None yet

Every figure on this site is provisional until hand-verified. Where a number appears, the page says how it was produced.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New here? Overview, then How we got here.
  • Method? Pipeline, Schema, Validation.
  • What has actually been run? Experiments and the friction log.
  • Why was X decided? Decision records.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Initiated statute. A citizen-proposed ordinary law enacted by popular vote. The unit this project studies. Constitutional amendments are out of scope because legislatures cannot unilaterally alter them.

Direct / indirect initiative. Describes the path to the ballot only. Direct goes straight to voters; indirect goes to the legislature first. Post-enactment alteration applies to both.

Adopt and amend. A legislature adopts an indirect initiative before the election to keep it off the ballot, then amends it under a lower threshold. Michigan, 2018.

Witness. One version of a legal text: the voter-enacted measure, an amending bill, or the current statute.

Base witness. The voter-enacted text. Spine IDs are assigned here and never change.

Spine ID. A persistent, human-legible provision identifier, e.g. MO-2024-PropA-p017: state, approval year, measure slug, zero-padded provision number in reading order.

Provision. One separately survivable unit of law. See the separate-survivability test below.

Separate-survivability test. An enumerated item is its own provision if the legislature could delete it while leaving its siblings intact and have the result make sense. Otherwise it is a component.

Component. An item that completes its parent provision. Kept as a record, flagged counts_in_denominator: false, with parent_spine_id set.

Provenance. Whether a provision was created by the measure, amended by it, or merely reprinted (inherited) from earlier law. Only created and amended provisions count toward survival.

Denominator. Records with counts_in_denominator == true and provenance created or amended.

Survival. What happened to a provision between the base witness and a comparison witness. Time-indexed: it can differ at each witness.

Dependency. A provision whose operation relies on another (a cross-reference, formula, or defined term). Recorded in depends_on.

Exemption sweep. A pipeline step that searches the whole amended statute for limiting language aimed at provisions that look intact.

Hybrid retrieval. Dense (embedding) search plus sparse (BM25 keyword) search, fused by reciprocal rank fusion.

Alignment. Matching an original provision to its counterpart in the amended text, or to none.

Gold. Hand-coded records, the ground truth the pipeline is measured against. Written by a human only.

Dev / held-out split. Gold used to tune the pipeline versus gold never touched until the pipeline is frozen.

Friction log. A running record of every place the schema failed to fit real statutory text.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
A parking lot for ideas that come up during the work and are not pressing. Nothing here is a decision. When an idea is adopted, it moves into the plan (docs/workflow/plan.md) with an ADR, and its entry here is marked as moved.

Format: date, idea, why it might matter, when it could fit.

docs.title: Ideas
docs.text:
2026-11-15. Side-by-side text in a dropdown panel. On the site, each provision opens an expandable panel showing the voter-enacted text and the amending text side by side. Why: it is the core reading experience for a scholar checking a claim. Fits: the website prototype now, and the real site later.

2026-11-15. Form-style coding screen. A local page for hand-coding gold: voter text and amending text side by side, a dropdown for each layer built from the closed value lists, saving to gold/ only on a human's input. Why: more intuitive than spreadsheet tabs and enforces the closed lists. Fits: after the site prototype, before the main gold coding. Note: the rule that agents never write to gold/ still applies. The tool would only record what the human selects.

2026-11-15. Ballotpedia links on every corpus row. Store the link and our own coded fields, never copied Ballotpedia text (their reuse terms apply the GFDL when text is copied). No API key is needed for links. Fits: corpus construction.

2026-11-15. Other model families as judges. Gemini and ChatGPT, alongside cross-checks between Claude models. Each judge is validated against the hand-coded gold before it is trusted, and a judge from a different family than the coder is preferred. Fits: after the pipeline exists.

2026-11-15. Corpus in two forms. A scrollable page on the site plus a data file on GitHub, with a page per initiative. Fits: corpus construction and the real site.

2026-11-15. Time-indexed view. Show how a law erodes across successive amending bills, not only its state after one bill. Follows from indexing outcomes by bill. Fits: the real site.

2026-11-15. Post-cutoff list display. A visible list of initiatives altered after the December 31, 2025 cutoff. Fits: corpus and site.

Earlier. Justification analysis. How legislators publicly justify overriding a popular vote (floor statements, committee testimony, sponsor memos). Deferred on retrieval cost. Fits: after the core corpus is coded. To be raised again when that stage arrives.

Earlier. Vehicle choice, large-n. Code every initiative in the initiative states on one dimension: statutory or constitutional. Several hundred measures. Makes the escalation cycle measurable. Fits: beyond the semester.

Earlier. Citable archive and license. A Zenodo DOI through GitHub releases, and a license choice for code and for data. Fits: before the site is called finished.

Earlier. A paper on the side. Personal project, not part of the capstone. Revisit much later.

2026-11-15. Check the Manifesto Project's document viewer. It codes party manifestos sentence by sentence and could be a useful reference. It could not be fetched during research. Fits: design references.

docs.title: Brief: "What Survives" website prototype (one session, tonight)
docs.text: You are building a local-only prototype of the project's website. The point of this session is to get the design and aesthetics right while a stronger model is available. Another model will continue the work afterwards, so everything you decide must be written down. The author presents this to a professor tomorrow, so it must work and look finished, and it must be honest about what the data is.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project measures what survives when a legislature alters an initiated statute, provision by provision. The final output is this website, modeled on the Frankenstein Variorum (frankensteinvariorum.org): a browsable, scholarly tool where the eye finds the hot spots, usable by scholars for real analysis. Think of it as a critical edition of a law, showing the version voters enacted against the version the legislature left.

Route A and Route B are a core part of the project. Every initiative has an enacted_by value: - Route A, enacted by voters: voters passed it, then the legislature altered it. The claim "what voters voted for" applies. - Route B, enacted by the legislature: the legislature adopted the initiative itself to keep it off the ballot (Michigan 2018 is the example), then altered it. Voters never voted, so the claim does not apply, and the two routes are never pooled in a statistic.

The route must be visible and meaningful everywhere: a badge on every case, a filter on every list, separate counts, and a plain-language explanation on the About and Method pages.

docs.title: Hard constraints
docs.text:
1. Local only. Never deploy or publish. Do not touch the docs workflow. Everything goes in site-prototype/.
  2. Read-only data. Do not modify or write anything in data/, gold/ or spec/. Read from them in place by serving the repo root. The one new data file you may create is site-prototype/data/corpus-seed.json (see the seed table below).
  3. Label everything. A persistent banner on every page: "Prototype. Model-coded, unaudited." Never call the data findings or results.
  4. Never reword source text. Quoted spans from voter text and bills are displayed exactly as stored.
  5. Compute, don't hardcode. Every count is computed from data. Denominator rule: counts_in_denominator == true AND provenance in (created, amended).
  6. No fabricated data, ever. If a view needs data we do not have (for example, a multi-bill timeline, or a Route B case), show an honest empty state. The empty state must say "Not coded yet" in those words, followed by a short line on what is needed. Never invent a record to fill a view. Every case, view or section without coded data says "Not coded yet", including every Route B case.
  7. No build step. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules). Vendor any library into the repo so it runs offline.
  8. Isolate data loading in site-prototype/js/data.js. The schema is about to change from one flat record per provision to four linked tables (initiative, bill, provision, outcome). Only data.js should need to change when it does.
  9. Run git switch -c site-prototype first. Commit often. Do not push to main. Do not push at all unless told.

docs.title: Step 0: Read before doing anything
docs.text:
Read CLAUDE.md, GLOSSARY.md, docs/method/schema.md, docs/workflow/plan.md (if present), docs/planning.md (if present), and docs/design/references.md. In spec/v1/01-Project-Context-What-Survives.txt, read section 9 (schema) and section 13 (site structure). Then inspect the data: - data/missouri-prop-a/coding/prop-a-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json - data/south-dakota-im22/coding/im22-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json

Check each file's coded_by values and report them. Write the actual field names you find to docs/design/data-contract.md. Do not rely on any field name from this brief; the files are the truth.

Create site-prototype/HANDOFF.md immediately and update it after every milestone: what is built, what is next, known issues, how to run it. If you are cut off, the next model resumes from it.

docs.title: Step 1: Study the references (visually, not just as text)
docs.text: Study the Frankenstein Variorum first and properly, because it is the model for this site. Then study the other sites in docs/design/references.md (Constitute, V-Dem Graphing Tools, Voteview, Comparative Agendas Project, Juxta, and the Legislative Influence Detector). Look at each for inspiration, not only the Variorum. Also study the author's four named style examples (listed in Step 3: Our World in Data, ACLED, MIT Election Lab). You may also look for other sites you think are relevant, within the usage limit. - Screenshots may be in docs/design/refs/ (images). Read them. Name which screenshots you used. - If a browser tool is available in this session (Claude in Chrome or similar), use it to open the Variorum and look at its visualization and reading views. - If neither is available, say so, and work from the descriptions and any text you can fetch. Do not pretend you saw an interface you did not. - Add a short note to references.md on what you actually borrowed. Do not copy any site's layout or branding.

docs.title: Step 2: Brainstorm (bounded, brief)
docs.text: Before writing the design spec, spend a short, bounded effort on your own concept thinking. Generate three genuinely different directions for the look and interaction of the site, critique each, choose one, and say why. You may propose additions or changes to the concept below and flag problems with it. You may not drop a required feature. Record this in a "Brainstorm" section of docs/design/DESIGN.md. Keep it to the point: this is not the main event.

docs.title: Step 3: Write docs/design/DESIGN.md before any code
docs.text:
Pages and views, interactions, which data field each view reads, the aesthetic direction and why (typography, color, spacing, light and dark), accessibility (contrast, color-blind-safe encodings, keyboard use), responsive behavior, and how Route A and B appear everywhere. Make it complete enough that another model can continue without asking you.

Aesthetic goal: the best, most distinctive result you can make. The author wants the visualizations to look very modern and very academic: clean and current, with the seriousness of a research publication. Calm, scholarly, typographic, closer to a critical edition than a dashboard. Avoid a templated look.

The author named these sites as visual examples. Study them (screenshots may be in docs/design/refs/, or open them if a browser tool is available) and say in DESIGN.md what you take from each. Borrow qualities, never layouts or branding: - https://ourworldindata.org/democracy - https://acleddata.com/ - https://electionlab.mit.edu/ - https://ourworldindata.org/

docs.title: Step 4: Build
docs.text:
Commit after each item. If time or usage runs short, stop at the highest-priority item completed, and make sure the site at that point works end to end.

Priority 1: the core 1. Case page. Header with title, route badge, status, and a link out when one exists. One strip of cells per case, one cell per provision in reading order. A lens switch colors the strip by Layer 1 (what happened, default), Layer 3 (direction), Layer 2 (type), or Layer 4 (mechanism). Components (counts_in_denominator == false) are visibly distinct. Inherited text (provenance == inherited) is visibly marked. A summary band shows computed counts and states the denominator rule in one line. Equal-width cells by default. 2. Side-by-side dropdown panel. Clicking a cell expands a panel showing the voter-enacted text and the amending text side by side, with the layer values, the rationale and the quoted evidence. This is a firm requirement. 3. Facts only / with interpretation toggle. One switch hides Layers 3 and 4 and shows only structural facts (Layers 1 and 2). It lets a reader who disputes our judgments still use the tool. 4. Dependency overlay. Show the link from a provision to what it depends on (depends_on, depended_on_by). Flag "hidden change" where dependency_affected is true (Missouri p003 is the example).

Priority 2: the corpus and the framing 5. Corpus page. A scrollable table seeded from corpus-seed.json, with route filter, status filter, and badges. Candidate rows are clearly marked as not yet coded. Rows link out to Ballotpedia where a link exists. 6. About page. The claim in plain language (marked provisional), the two routes explained, and a section on trustworthiness: how coding was done (model-coded versus hand-verified), what the limits are, and why every figure is labeled. 7. Method page. The layers in plain language, the closed value lists (with each value one click from where it is used), the provision rule, the denominator rule, and the cutoff (December 31, 2025).

Priority 3: cross-case and extras (build those the data supports; empty states for the rest) 8. Corpus small multiples. Every coded case as one strip, stacked, sortable by year, route, or topic, so the eye finds patterns across cases. 9. Description versus effect. For each bill, show how the bill described itself next to what it did, if the data has it. Otherwise an empty state. 10. Mechanism matrix. Mechanisms against cases, clickable down to the provisions. 11. Speed view. Days from enactment to alteration per case, with a mark for whether the provision had taken effect, if the data supports it. 12. Erosion timeline. Stacked strips for the law at enactment, after bill 1, after bill 2. Needs multi-bill data. Build the empty state and the design, show no fake data. 13. Visible controls. A designed slot for unaltered and technical-correction cases, which do not exist in the data yet. Empty state only. 14. Citation and export. A permalink for every provision, a "cite this" button, and CSV and JSON download of the current view. 15. Length-weighted cell width. An optional, clearly labeled toggle. Equal width stays the default, because width could imply severity and the project deliberately has no severity score.

Do not build a trust-badge display on the visualization. Trustworthiness is explained on the About page. The persistent "model-coded, unaudited" banner stays.

docs.title: Step 5: Verify
docs.text:
• Write site-prototype/check_data.py that prints the counts the site should show. Confirm the site matches it.
  • Expected for Missouri Prop A, to be verified, not assumed: 102 records, 70 with counts_in_denominator == true, 32 components. MO-2024-PropA-p003 should show partially deleted, narrows, escalation removal, and dependency_affected true.
  • If you can run a browser (for example Playwright), screenshot at desktop and narrow widths and review against DESIGN.md. Otherwise say you could not.
  • Report any mismatch between what the display needs and what the schema provides, and add each as an entry to docs/log/friction-log.md.

docs.title: Step 6: Finish
docs.text: Update HANDOFF.md. Commit on the site-prototype branch. Give the exact command to run it: python3 -m http.server 8000 from the repo root, then open http://localhost:8000/site-prototype/.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Deployment, a backend, user accounts, editing data, the real corpus, anything that changes the schema.

docs.title: Design references
docs.text: Researched November 15, 2026 from each site's own descriptive pages. The descriptions below come from page text, not from looking at the interfaces. Open each one yourself before relying on it. None of these is to be copied. The point is to borrow ideas.

docs.title: 1. Constitute (constituteproject.org)
docs.text: Built by the Comparative Constitutions Project. Passages of the world's constitutions are tagged with 300+ topics. Users search by topic, filter by region and period, and read in a List view or a Compare view that puts two constitutions side by side. Excerpts can be pinned and exported to Google Docs, PDF or CSV. Every search, comparison and provision has a deep link. - Closest match to what we are building: tagged legal text, side by side. - Borrow: topic tags as a way in, deep links to a single provision, pinning and export. - Avoid: a search-first design. Ours should let the eye find hot spots before any search.

docs.title: 2. V-Dem Graphing Tools (v-dem.net/graphingtools.html)
docs.text: Expert-coded democracy indicators, shown through many views: map, line graph, radar, scatter, heat map, regional and thematic comparison between two years. - Borrow: the idea of several views over one dataset, and a before-and-after comparison between two points in time. This maps onto comparing a law before and after an amending bill. - Avoid: a menu of a dozen chart types. We need one primary view done very well.

docs.title: 3. Voteview (voteview.com)
docs.text: UCLA's tool for every congressional roll call vote in history, shown on a US map and on an ideological map of legislators. Search and download tools are included. - Borrow: one spatial picture that makes a whole dataset legible at a glance, with every point clickable down to the underlying record. - Avoid: abstract scaling that readers must trust. Our encodings should be readable without a methods paper.

docs.title: 4. Comparative Agendas Project (comparativeagendas.net)
docs.text: Policy activity coded into 20 major topics and 200+ subtopics, with a Trends Tool for graphing coded series over time for one country or several. - Borrow: a coded dataset that non-specialists can explore, and an honest codebook linked from the tool. - Avoid: a codebook that readers must leave the tool to understand.

docs.title: 5. Juxta Commons (digital humanities text collation)
docs.text: A tool for comparing versions of a text. It offers three views: a heat map that overlays the texts and colors differences, a side-by-side view with lines connecting points of difference, and a histogram showing which portions changed most. - Borrow: the heat map as the first view, with the histogram idea as an at-a-glance summary of where change concentrated. This is closest to the Frankenstein Variorum approach. - Caution: the page describes a 2013 poster abstract. Check juxtasoftware.org for whether the tool is still available.

docs.title: Bonus: Legislative Influence Detector (DSSG fellowship)
docs.text: Finds text reused between state bills and model legislation. Results appear side by side with matching passages highlighted. - Borrow: highlighted overlap between two legal texts. - Caution: the page is a project writeup from about 2015 to 2018, and I could not confirm the live tool still works.

docs.title: What these suggest for our site
docs.text:
• Lead with an at-a-glance picture (heat map or strip), with detail one click away.
  • Make the side-by-side comparison of two legal texts the core reading view.
  • Give every provision a stable link.
  • Keep the codebook one click from every coded value.
  • Show how change concentrates, not only whether it occurred.

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
Everything that was tried, decided, or got in the way.

  • Experiments
  • Decision records
  • Schema changelog
  • Friction log
  • Timing

Entries are dated, and are not edited after the fact. A correction is a new entry that points at the old one.

docs.title: Friction log
docs.text: Places where the schema or method failed to fit real text. These are results.

docs.title: Missouri Prop A prototype
docs.text:
1. Inherited text. The certified measure reprints statutory sections including 2006 language. Counting it inflates survival. Fixed by adding provenance.

2. Hidden dependency. Provision p003 points at p002 for its escalation formula, so p003 can be textually intact and substantively changed. Fixed by adding depends_on.

3. No Layer 4 value for escalation removal. HB 567 removed indexing clauses while keeping step increases. The schema could not name it, even though indexing removal is the pattern the central hypothesis predicts. Value added.

4. Dependency field in the wrong block. dependency_affected was nested inside exemption_sweep, mixing a hand-derived finding with a machine sweep result. Separated.

5. Definition sub-items inflated the denominator. 38 of 102 records were definitional. Resolved by flagging instead of merging, which kept spine IDs stable.

6. The provision rule keyed on typography. Lettered sub-items were treated as components. Section 290.603(4)'s lettered paragraphs are each separately survivable, while section 290.630(2)'s complete one sentence. Replaced with the separate-survivability test. Section 290.606(7) was the first list that split across the test.

7. Task scope error. A fix task named 23 sub-items when the file contained 39 two-level records. Tasks are now written as rules, not ID lists.

8. Layer 4 never discriminated. It took one value on 99 of 102 records because the bill repealed the sections wholesale. A property of the case. Resolved by case selection.

docs.title: Schema friction log — What Survives
docs.text: Tracks changes to the 9-layer coding schema and record template discovered during prototype-stage hand-coding (not bugs — the prototype's whole purpose is to surface exactly this kind of friction before the schema is locked for the full corpus).

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — Two issues found during Missouri Proposition A hand-coding
docs.text: Source: schema-fixes-prop-a.md (Andrew, from reading the certified initiative text while hand-coding). Both required changes to prop-a-provisions-scaffold.json and prop-a-structural-outline.md.

docs.title: Issue 1 — Corpus mixes three provenances
docs.text:
01-initiative-text.md is the certified measure as printed, which reprints entire statutory sections verbatim, including language inherited from earlier enactments. Example: MO-2024-PropA-p001 (290.502(1), the $6.50/2007 baseline) is 2006 ballot-measure language carried forward, not text Proposition A wrote. Counting unchanged inherited text as "survived" inflates the survival-rate metric — it isn't evidence that voters' 2024 choices were preserved, since Prop A didn't choose that text in the first place.

Fix applied: Added provenance (created | amended | inherited | uncertain) and provenance_basis (free text) fields to every record, immediately after measure_id. Survival-rate denominators will include only created and amended records; inherited stays visible in the case view flagged as context; uncertain is reported as a coverage gap rather than silently dropped or silently counted. Documented in prop-a-structural-outline.md.

Status: Schema change applied (scaffold + outline). Assigning the actual provenance value per chunk is hand-coding work — Andrew's, not the pipeline's or mine — and proceeds separately, chunk by chunk, per the prototype spec's division of labor.

docs.title: Issue 2 — Provisions depend on other provisions
docs.text:
MO-2024-PropA-p003 (290.502(3), the Prop A wage schedule) does not contain its own escalation formula — it incorporates it by reference ("per the method set forth in subsection 2," i.e. p002). A provision's own text can be unchanged while its operative effect changes completely because something it depends on was altered. Comparing p003 to its counterpart in isolation, ignoring p002's alteration, would misscore it as intact. This is the exemption-sweep pass/fail criterion from the prototype spec, in its first live instance.

Fix applied: Added depends_on (list of spine IDs, hand-assigned by reading the base witness alone, before opening the comparison witness) and depended_on_by (inverted mechanically once hand-coding is complete) after comparison_witness. Added dependency_affected (bool) and dependency_source_ids (list) inside exemption_sweep — the sweep now checks two things, not one: limiting language added elsewhere in the amended statute, AND alteration of any provision in depends_on.

Status: Schema change applied. p003 is the named benchmark case for prototype acceptance criterion 5 (the exemption sweep) — its Layer 1/Layer 3 reasoning, and its depends_on: [MO-2024-PropA-p002] relationship to the now-narrowed CPI clause, is the test case for whether the sweep logic actually works once the pipeline runs.

docs.title: Coding-order instruction (from Andrew, logged for continuity)
docs.text: Fields are coded one at a time across all 102 chunks, not one record at a time — per-record coding lets judgment criteria drift unnoticed across a long chunk sequence; coding one field at a time keeps the criterion fixed while it's being applied. provenance and depends_on are coded first, reading the base witness only (HB 567 not yet open), before any comparison layers are touched.

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — Provenance re-derived from an actual prior-statute diff; one guess corrected
docs.text:
Earlier provenance values for p001–p004 (in the worked example only) were assigned by reasoning from the legislative-history note and a guess at what subsection 4 probably said before 2024 — p004 was marked amended at "medium confidence," flagged as "not independently verified." Andrew asked for a real diff: 00-prior-statute-2023.md (RSMo 290.500–290.530 as in force December 2023, pulled from revisor.mo.gov's historical bid versions) was added as the base witness, and 01-initiative-text.md was re-derived to preserve the certified PDF's own bracket markup ([deleted] / plain-unbracketed-retained-or- added) for the one section Prop A amended, 290.502.

Checked first whether the certified PDF uses underline/strikethrough as hypothesized: it does not (confirmed via font-level inspection, not just visual read — every character in the amended subsection renders in one plain, non-bold font). It uses Missouri's standard bracket-for-deletion bill-drafting convention instead, with no distinct marking for additions.

The diff against subsection 4 showed it is byte-identical to the pre-2024 text — zero bracket markers. p004's provenance is inherited, not amended. The earlier guess was wrong. p001, p002 (also zero brackets) confirmed inherited; p003 (five bracket deletions) confirmed amended. provenance for all 102 chunks is now set in both prop-a-provisions-scaffold.json and prop-a-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json, using the diff method for p001–p004 and "enacting new section, no prior counterpart exists" for p005–p102. prop-a-structural-outline.md now carries inline [CREATED]/[AMENDED]/[INHERITED] and [DEPENDED-ON-BY: ...] tags per chunk as a reading aid, sourced from the EXAMPLE file (the only one with depends_on populated so far).

Lesson: a provenance guess reasoned from surrounding context, without checking the actual prior text, got the benchmark-adjacent record wrong. Diff against a real base witness before assigning provenance, even when the guess seems well-supported.

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — Layer 6/7/8 bill-level/measure-level gaps filled (EXAMPLE only)
docs.text:
Filled the remaining null sub-fields in layer_6_temporal_procedural, layer_7_measure_context, and layer_8_subsequent_fate across all 102 records of prop-a-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json (scaffold untouched — these fields are hand-coding work for Andrew there, per the established division of labor). Because these fields are "scope": "bill-level" / "measure-level", this was ~11 real-world research lookups applied uniformly, not 102 judgment calls.

Sources (WebSearch, 2026-10-05): HB 567 introduced Dec 16, 2024; House passed 84-62 (Mar 13, 2025); Senate passed 22-11 (May 14, 2025); House Committee on Commerce recommended Do Pass Feb 27, 2025 (also Committee on Legislative Review, 7-3, Mar 5, 2025) — replaces the prior "NOT_RETRIEVABLE" sentinel for committee_of_origin. Governor signed July 10, 2025; effective Aug 28, 2025 (confirms existing emergency_clause: false). Support campaign "Missourians for Healthy Families & Fair Wages" raised ~$6M (incl. $500K Sixteen Thirty Fund, $250K Open Society Policy Center); opposition total not found in available sources, left unquantified rather than guessed. Missouri Supreme Court, 5-2, April 29, 2025: upheld Prop A against a post-election challenge (business groups incl. Missouri Chamber of Commerce, NFIB) to the ballot summary/fiscal note; declined jurisdiction over the single-subject claim post-election. A 2026 constitutional amendment campaign ("Missouri Minimum Wage Amendment" / Initiative Petition 2026-047) is circulating, signature deadline May 3, 2026, targeting the Nov 3, 2026 ballot.

days_enactment_to_introduction = 41, computed as Nov 5, 2024 (election/certification date — confirmed as this schema's "enactment" anchor by reverse-engineering the pre-existing days_enactment_to_alteration_effective: 296 value) to Dec 16, 2024 (HB 567 introduction).

Two sub-fields deliberately left null, not guessed: - supermajority_met — supermajority_required is false for this measure type (ordinary statute, simple-majority override), so "was a supermajority met" has no defined meaning here; encoding true or false would imply a threshold that doesn't apply. Left null as not-applicable rather than computing the numeric coincidence that the Senate margin (22-11) happens to equal 2/3 while the House margin (84-62) does not. - provision_reenacted_substantially_same — the 2026 constitutional-amendment campaign has not yet reached a ballot or taken effect as of this research pass; nothing exists yet to compare against for "substantially the same" text. Genuinely unresolved, not unresearched.

Both are honest gaps per the project's established convention, not defects.

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — South Dakota Initiated Measure 22 (2016) case built: scope, markup, and gaps
docs.text: Second case study built at data/south-dakota-im22/, mirroring the Prop A pipeline (sources/00-04, coding/im22-structural-outline.md, im22-provisions-scaffold.json, im22-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json). Andrew confirmed the coding-format split (scaffold + EXAMPLE, same as Prop A) and the scope decision below before work started.

docs.title: Scope decision: all three categories HB 1069 touches
docs.text:
Before coding, a lookup was run (at Andrew's request) to check whether HB 1069 (2017), the bill that repealed IM 22, treated all of IM 22's text uniformly. It does not. HB 1069 touches three distinct categories: 1. The wholly new SDCL ch. 12-28 (independent ethics commission, democracy-credit public financing, disclosure regime) — repealed outright. 2. New sections IM 22 added into the existing ch. 12-27 — also repealed outright. 3. ~23 pre-existing SDCL sections IM 22 had amended (ch. 12-27 contribution/disclosure sections, ch. 2-12 lobbying/revolving-door sections) — HB 1069 amends these again rather than repealing them.

Category 3 is the only part of this case with partial-survival nuance comparable to Prop A; categories 1-2 are a clean "total repeal" story. Andrew chose to include all three categories rather than narrow scope, specifically because of that asymmetry.

docs.title: Markup convention: confirmed by the source document itself, then cross-validated
docs.text: Unlike Missouri (where the convention had to be discovered via font-level PDF inspection), the IM 22 transcription used as the base source states its own convention in its header: overstrike = deleted from existing law, underline = added to existing law. Confirmed structurally this pass by cross-checking two independent documents: resolving the certified-text file's own §4 (12-27-1) to its post-IM22 state and the HB-1069-enacted file's §3 to its pre-HB1069 state — which describe the same statute text at the handoff moment — produced near-identical text (12,141 vs. 12,146 characters, differing only in whitespace/bill- preamble noise). The two independently-sourced documents agree.

docs.title: Deliberate deviations from the Prop A pipeline (flagged honestly, not silently)
docs.text:
• Official SOS certified-text PDF not retrieved. https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/assets/InitiatedMeasure22.pdf returned HTTP 404; no working URL pattern was found within this research budget. Used the Dakota Free Press transcription (sourced from the measure's own sponsoring campaign committee) instead. Documented in 01-initiative-text.md's header.
  • Pre-2016 baseline (00-prior-statute-2016.md) is reconstructed, not independently fetched. South Dakota's historical-statute tool is a JS-rendered SPA inaccessible to this pipeline's fetch tools (unlike Missouri's revisor.mo.gov, which exposes per-section historical versions directly). The baseline is instead reconstructed by resolving the certified text's own strike/underline markup to its PRE state. Weaker evidence than Missouri's independently-sourced base witness; flagged in the file header.
  • Chunking stopped at IM 22's own "Section N" unit (70 chunks), not sub-section/lettered granularity. IM 22's text is much longer than Prop A's; splitting to the same granularity Prop A used would have produced several hundred chunks. Flagged in the structural outline's header as a scope/effort tradeoff, not hidden.
  • Ch. 12-28 per-subsection SDCL citations are approximate ("12-28-X (approx.)"). HB 1069's repeal list confirms the aggregate range (§12-28-1, §§12-28-2 to 12-28-37) but this pass did not individually re-derive which IM-22 "Section N" became which exact 12-28-N from the official Session Laws codification table. Confirmed precisely: IM22 §1 (short title) = 12-28-1 (direct match in HB1069's repeal list and in a Justia search-result snippet).
  • layer_2_provision_type values are descriptive labels ("disclosure/reporting requirement", "enforcement/penalty", "institutional/administrative", "public financing mechanism", "conduct restriction"), not drawn from a confirmed master enum — this pass only had Prop A's four observed values ("rate, amount, or threshold", "escalation, indexing, or adjustment", "definitions", plus implied others) to go on, and none fit most of IM 22's content. Flagged for Andrew to reconcile against the real schema enum if one exists beyond what's been observed in the Prop A files.

docs.title: Genuine edge case found: two "revived citation" records (p017, p018)
docs.text: IM 22 itself repealed two pre-existing sections outright (12-27-17, 12-27-17.1) rather than amending them — a repeal nested inside the initiative, not something HB 1069 did. HB 1069 then enacted new text under those same two citations (confirmed via HB 1069 §17's own text, which cross-references "§ 12-27-17" as an existing citation) — not a restoration of the pre-2016 original. This doesn't cleanly fit the created/amended/inherited provenance enum or the structural-operation enum (unchanged/rewritten/partially deleted/deleted entirely). Classified provenance "amended" and structural operation "rewritten" as closest fits, with the full reasoning left in each record's layer_3_rationale rather than smoothed over. Same spirit as Prop A's p003 bundling note — a real schema boundary case worth the user's attention, not a coding error.

docs.title: Diff-based partial-survival finding (the point of including category 3)
docs.text: Of the 23 category-3 "amended again" sections, diffing HB 1069's resulting text against the reconstructed pre-2016 baseline shows only 6 sections reverted byte-for-byte to the pre-IM22 original (12-27-11, 12-27-12, 12-27-13, 12-27-21, 12-27-37, 2-12-8.2). The other 17 show a text-length delta against the pre-2016 baseline, meaning either some IM-22-originated language survived HB 1069's rewrite, or HB 1069 drafted genuinely new (non-restorative) 2017 language, or both. This pass did not hand-verify which of those two explanations applies clause-by-clause for each of the 17 — that is real hand-coding work, flagged in each affected record (confidence: "low", flagged_for_review: true) rather than guessed at. 19 of 70 EXAMPLE records carry this flag (the 17 partial-reversion sections plus the 2 revived-citation sections).

docs.title: Layer 6-8 bill/measure-level fields: filled via real sourcing, same as Prop A
docs.text:
IM 22 enacted/certified Nov. 16, 2016 (enactment anchor, same convention as Prop A). HB 1069 introduced Jan. 20, 2017 (65 days later); House 54-13 (Jan 24), Senate 27-8 (Feb 1); signed Feb 2, 2017 (78 days after enactment); emergency clause: true — this is the case's defining fact, specifically invoked to foreclose a people's-veto referendum, confirmed set referendum_filed_against_alteration: false for that reason rather than "none found." Litigation: enjoined but never finally decided on the merits (mooted by the repeal) — struck_down: false, full reasoning in litigation_outcome. Subsequent similar measure: 2018 Amendment W, confirmed defeated 45.06%-54.94% — unlike Prop A's still-pending 2026 campaign, this subsequent measure's outcome is already known, so provision_reenacted_substantially_same: false (not left null) for all records. Campaign funding: Represent.Us contributed ~$1M (57% of support-side total, implying ~$1.75M raised); opposition total not found, left unquantified. committee_of_origin filled (House State Affairs, Senate State Affairs) rather than left as the "NOT_RETRIEVABLE" sentinel Prop A needed.

Final provenance counts (both files, identical): created 45, amended 25 (23 ordinary amendments + 2 revived-citation edge cases), inherited 0 — no inherited records in this case, because every one of the 70 chunks either adds new law or demonstrably changes pre-existing text (confirmed per-section via strike/ underline presence, not assumed from the "be amended" label alone — the same check that caught Prop A's p004 error was re-run here and found all 23 "amended" sections genuinely contain diff markers).

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — Three issues found reviewing prop-a-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json by hand
docs.text: Source: numbered task list from Andrew, after reading the EXAMPLE file himself. All three required changes to prop-a-provisions-EXAMPLE-coded.json; the first also required a new codebook.md (none existed before this).

docs.title: Issue 1 — Layer 4 lacked a mechanism for escalation removal
docs.text: MO-2024-PropA-p003 was coded layer_1_structural_operation: "partially deleted" but layer_4_mechanism: "outright repeal" — contradictory, since HB 567 deleted the two post-2026 CPI indexing clauses from this provision while retaining its $13.75 → $15.00 step increases verbatim. Notable beyond this one record: indexing/escalation removal while retaining the underlying substantive rate is exactly the pattern the project's central hypothesis predicts (text survives, operative effect doesn't) — and the schema as designed had no name for it. Added escalation removal to the Layer 4 enum (codebook.md); re-coded p003 to it; added a validation rule (layer_4_mechanism == "outright repeal" implies layer_1_structural_operation == "deleted entirely", else flag inconsistent) and re-ran it against all 102 records: 0 inconsistencies after the fix.

docs.title: Issue 2 — dependency_affected was nested inside exemption_sweep
docs.text: All 102 records have exemption_sweep.ran: false, yet p003 reported a dependency finding (dependency_affected: true, source p002) inside that same object — conflating a hand-derived finding from the depends_on graph with a machine exemption-sweep result, which are different operations with different inputs. Moved dependency_affected / dependency_source_ids to two new top-level fields (positioned after depended_on_by) on all 102 records; exemption_sweep now holds only sweep-proper fields (ran, limiting_language_found, limiting_source_citation, limiting_span, reclassified_from). p003's existing values were preserved at the new location.

docs.title: Issue 3 — The mechanical split inflated the survival denominator with definition sub-items
docs.text:
38 of 102 records are definitional (290.600's defined-term list); 23 of those are lettered sub-items of three parent terms (290.600(5), 12 sub-items; 290.600(7), 5; 290.600(11), 6) — e.g. 290.600(5)(A). Counting each sub-item as a separately survivable provision inflates the denominator: a defined term with 6 lettered clauses weighs 6x a one-sentence provision in the survival-rate metric, for no principled reason. Resolved by flagging rather than merging, which preserves spine IDs and traceability: added parent_spine_id (null by default) and counts_in_denominator (true by default) to every record; set counts_in_denominator: false and parent_spine_id to the parent's spine ID for the 23 sub-items; rolled the depends_on of the 5 sub-items that had any (p029, p036, p037, p038, p039) up into their parents (p024, p033), deduplicated, then re-derived depended_on_by for all 102 by inversion — 0 mismatches after re-derivation. The survival-rate denominator rule is now: a record counts only if counts_in_denominator == true AND provenance IN ("created", "amended"). This produced the project's working answer to the prototype specification's open question "what is a provision" (documented in prop-a-structural-outline.md): a defined term is one provision; its lettered sub-items are components, not separately survivable units.

Verification note: before applying Issue 3's fix, re-checked (did not just trust) the claim that no record outside the 23 depends on a sub-item and no sub-item has any depended_on_by — confirmed true across all 102 records. Also audited every one of the 102 layer_1_structural_ operation values against base_witness vs. comparison_witness (HB 567) rather than against 00-prior-statute-2023.md, since MO-2024-PropA-p002 (inherited, byte-identical to the pre-2024 statute) is coded rewritten, which is coherent only if Layer 1 reflects HB 567's treatment, not the earlier diff. Result: 0 mismatches — HB 567 repealed all of 290.502 and re-enacted one new section, so p001 (byte-identical in both witnesses) is correctly unchanged while p002 and p004 (text changed by HB 567 despite being inherited provenance) are correctly rewritten. No re-coding required.

Not in scope (flagged, not fixed): Layer 4 took outright repeal on 99 of 102 records because HB 567 repealed the paid-sick-time sections wholesale — the layer never had to discriminate, and 17 of its 18 values (now that escalation removal exists) remain untested on real data. This is a property of the case, not a defect in the coding; resolved by second-case selection, not by editing this file further.

docs.title: 2026-10-05 — Correction: the provision rule from the previous entry was itself wrong
docs.text:
Source: Andrew, after re-reading the file and finding a conflict between that entry's Task 6 (flag only the 23 §290.600 definition sub-items) and Task 9 (state a general rule: any enumerated list elaborating one defined term or obligation is one provision). The file applied a narrow fix but documented a broad rule — 39 records in the file have two-level citations, and only 23 were flagged, so the stated rule and the actual data disagreed.

The initial provision rule keyed on typography — lettered sub-items were treated as components. Applying it to the full set of enumerated lists showed this was wrong: §290.603(4)'s lettered paragraphs each state an independent accrual rule and are separately survivable (accrual commencement, overtime-exempt treatment, carryover, inter-division transfer, successor-employer continuity, and employer-advanced loans are six unrelated rules, each a complete sentence/ paragraph on its own topic), while §290.630(2)'s lettered clauses complete a single sentence (one recordkeeping mandate: maintain separately, treat as confidential, and do not disclose) and cannot stand alone as independent rules. The rule was replaced with a separate-survivability test — deletable alone without leaving the provision incoherent — applied by reading the text rather than counting parenthesis levels (full rule text in prop-a-structural-outline.md, Task 12).

Re-applied to all 16 previously-unflagged two-level records (the 23 §290.600 definition sub-items were unaffected and remain flagged): - 290.630(2)(A)–(C) (p092–p094): components. Fragments of one sentence/obligation. - 290.606(1)(A)–(D) (p057–p060): components. Each item is a fragment of the single sentence "earned paid sick time shall be provided... for: (A)...(D)", enumerating the scope of one entitlement rather than stating independent rules. - 290.603(4)(A)–(F) (p047–p052): remain separate provisions, no change. Each is a complete, independent accrual rule on a distinct topic. - 290.606(7)(A)–(C) (p067–p069): split — the first case where one enumerated list divides across the test. (A) and (B) are both answers to the same question ("what counts as reasonable documentation," for the general case and the domestic-violence case respectively) and were treated as components of that single documentation-sufficiency provision (p066). (C) is a freestanding prohibition on the employer ("may not require that the documentation explain the nature of the illness...") — a different kind of rule, not a species of "what counts as reasonable" — and was left a separate provision, counts_in_denominator: true.

Dependencies for the 4 newly-flagged components with non-empty depends_on (p057–p060 had none; p068 did) were rolled up into their parents (p056 gained 3 deps from p060; p066 gained 4 deps from p068, one of which — p056 itself — is a dependency on the now-component-bearing parent record, left as-is since p066 and p056 are siblings in the same subsection, not a p066-on-itself cycle). depended_on_by was then re-derived for all 102 records by inverting depends_on: 0 mismatches. Also re-verified, across every record now carrying a parent_spine_id (not just the 4 newly rolled up), that each component's depends_on values are present in its parent's depends_on — confirmed for all, including the original 23 from the prior entry (the original Task 7 roll-up check could not have been meaningful for records where parent_spine_id was still null at the time it ran; re-running it now against the final state closes that gap).

Final counts after correction: counts_in_denominator: true — 70 records; false — 32 records (the original 23 §290.600 definition sub-items plus 9 more: 3 from 290.630(2), 4 from 290.606(1), 2 from 290.606(7)). Final survival-rate denominator (counts_in_denominator: true AND provenance IN ("created","amended")) = 67 records. By layer_2_provision_type: core obligation or entitlement 25, definitions 15, administrative procedure 8, conflict or preemption clause 8, enforcement authority 4, rulemaking authority and agency discretion 2, penalty or remedy 2, private right of action 2, escalation/indexing/adjustment 1.

Lesson: a rule stated in general terms (Task 9) was applied narrowly (Task 6), and the gap between the two went unnoticed until the file was re-read end to end. When a documented rule and the data it's supposed to govern disagree, re-run the rule against the full dataset rather than trusting that the first application was exhaustive.

docs.title: ADR 0001: What counts as a provision
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The mechanical split gave one record per definition sub-item, so 38 of 102 records were definitional and the survival denominator was dominated by vocabulary. A first rule based on typography was wrong.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A provision is a separately survivable unit. An enumerated item is its own provision if it could be deleted alone and leave a coherent statute. Otherwise it is a component, kept as a record with parent_spine_id set and counts_in_denominator: false.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Spine IDs are preserved and the rule is reversible. Applying the test needs reading the text and is a judgment, so it is a source of coder disagreement to measure.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Persistent spine IDs
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Alteration happens across several amending bills over time, and provisions are renumbered, split and merged. Tracking survival needs a stable referent.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Human-legible IDs are assigned once on the base witness (the voter text) and never reassigned. Provisions added by a legislature get IDs flagged as having no initiative counterpart. Restructuring is one-to-many.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Adapted from the Frankenstein Variorum collation model. Renumbering cannot silently break a record.

docs.title: ADR 0003: A layered schema with no severity field
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A single label such as altered cannot separate a technical fix from a gutting. A severity score would encode the researcher's judgment as a number.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Nine layers separate what the text did from what it means, from near-objective to interpretive. Prior and subsequent similar-measure years are stored, not thresholded. There is no severity field.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Readers judge how much a change matters. Interpretive layers are reported separately so their lower reliability is visible.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Gold is hand-coded
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Prop A prototype was coded by a model. Evaluating a model against model output would measure self-agreement.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Only human-coded records enter gold/, and no agent may write there. Model-coded files are labeled as such and never used as ground truth.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Hand-coding is a real cost and must be timed. A second coder is needed for a subset to establish a human ceiling.

docs.title: ADR 0005: Provenance and the survival denominator
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Certified measure text reprints earlier statute, so inherited text surviving says nothing about the voters' 2024 choice.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Every record carries provenance. Survival counts only records with counts_in_denominator == true and provenance created or amended. Inherited and uncertain records stay visible as context.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: On Prop A the denominator fell from 102 records to 67.

docs.title: ADR 0006: Diverse-case selection
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A small non-random set cannot support a claim of representativeness.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Cases are selected to span rule regime, domain, form of alteration and outcome. Criteria and exclusions are published. Counter-cases (technical correction, implementation, unaltered control) are mandatory. All eligible cases are machine-coded and about fifteen are hand-verified.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The paper claims coverage of the range of alteration, not a population estimate.

docs.title: E001 Missouri Prop A prototype
docs.text:
• Date: autumn 2026
  • Status: run, provisional
  • Schema version: 0.1, then 0.2 after fixes

Provisional. The coding was done by a model. No record was hand-coded, and no timing exists. Treat every figure here as a hypothesis.

docs.title: Hypothesis
docs.text: The prediction was selective partial hollowing: some provisions kept, others narrowed. The prediction was wrong.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: The Prop A certified text was split mechanically into 102 chunks, then coded across the nine layers.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• 102 records. Provenance counts were recorded as 98 / 1 / 3 (category order to be confirmed on audit)
  • Denominator after the provision rule: 67
  • 66 deleted entirely, 1 partially surviving (p003)
  • p003 survives textually but loses its post-2026 indexing, and also depends on a provision that was rewritten, so it narrows through two channels
  • Layer 4 took one value on 99 of 102 records

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Near-total deletion. The case is close to degenerate for testing the interpretive layers, so it cannot show that Layer 3 or 4 discriminate. It did show the schema gaps listed in the friction log.

docs.title: Consequence
docs.text: Schema v0.2. A second case with variation in mechanism is needed. Hand-coding must come before any pipeline evaluation.

docs.title: EXXX Title
docs.text:
• Date:
  • Status: planned / run / abandoned
  • Schema version:
  • Commit:

docs.title: Hypothesis
docs.text: What was expected, written before the run.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Inputs, model, parameters, split used.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Numbers, with how each was produced.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: What it means and what it does not.

docs.title: Consequence
docs.text: What changed because of it.

docs.title: Design
docs.text: The cases are chosen for diversity, not sampled. With a small, non-random set, a claim of representativeness would be false. The claim is instead that the cases span the dimensions along which alteration varies, and the criteria and exclusions are published so a reader can see what was left out.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
• Tier 1. Every eligible case is machine-coded by the pipeline.
  • Tier 2. About fifteen cases are hand-verified, and these carry the validation claims.

docs.title: Dimensions to span
docs.text:
• Rule regime: unrestricted, restricted, purpose-fidelity
  • Policy domain
  • Speed and form of alteration (immediate repeal, gradual amendment, adopt-and-amend)
  • Outcome (largely deleted, partly narrowed, largely preserved)

docs.title: Mandatory counter-cases
docs.text: Technical corrections, implementation bills, and unaltered controls. Without them, every case is one where something went wrong, and the method cannot show it distinguishes a hollowing from a fix.

docs.title: Candidates
docs.text:
All unverified. Each must be confirmed against primary sources before use.

Case Why it is a candidate Missouri Prop A (2024) Prototype case. Near-total deletion by HB 567, with one provision partially surviving. Layer 4 is almost untested here Missouri Prop B (2024) Intended second case, so Layer 4 gets variation South Dakota IM 22 (2016) Deletions and replacement, the benchmark for the none branch Michigan paid sick leave (2018) Adopt-and-amend, and a later judicial restoration Maine or another case A third regime

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text:
Constitutional amendments, local measures, and measures from before the chosen window. Excluded cases are listed on this page when decisions are made, with the reason.

See ADR 0006.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Status: designed, not built. Nothing on this page has been run. Each stage is specified so it can be built eval-first and tested against hand-coded gold.

Every stage writes to disk, can be re-run alone, and caches by input hash.

# Stage What it does Main failure it guards against 1 Decomposition Splits the voter-enacted text into provisions with persistent spine IDs Inconsistent unit of analysis 2 Hybrid retrieval For each provision, proposes candidate counterparts in the amended text Missing a moved or rewritten provision 3 Alignment adjudication An LLM picks the true counterpart from the candidates, or none Forcing a match onto a deleted provision 4 Effect classification Layer 1 (operation) and Layer 3 (direction), each with a rationale and a quoted span Unsupported judgments 5 Exemption sweep and dependency check Searches the whole amended statute for limiting language, and checks whether anything a provision depends on changed Provisions that look intact but are hollowed elsewhere 6 Layers 4 to 9 Mechanism, justification, procedure, measure context, subsequent fate, metadata 7 Validation Span verification, invariant tests, comparison to gold Hallucination, internal contradiction

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Hybrid retrieval. Two searches fused. Dense retrieval embeds each provision as a vector and finds near neighbours by meaning, so it finds a reworded provision. BM25 is keyword search, so it finds exact section numbers and defined terms. Reciprocal rank fusion merges the two ranked lists by position, with no score calibration. No vector database is needed at this corpus size.

Alignment with a none branch. The model is shown the original provision and the top candidates and must choose one or answer none. Without none, a deleted provision is paired with its nearest neighbour and scored as changed instead of deleted. The South Dakota IM 22 deletions are the benchmark.

Exemption sweep. A provision can be textually identical and still neutralised by a carve-out elsewhere. The sweep reads the full amended statute for language that limits the provision's reach.

Dependency check. If provision A computes something by reference to provision B and B changed, A has changed in effect even though its text did not. Missouri p003 is the benchmark.

Span verification. Every judgment must quote the supporting text with character offsets. Code checks that the quote matches the source exactly. This is the main hallucination guard.

Self-consistency. Each classification runs five times at low temperature, with candidate order shuffled to cancel position bias. Disagreement is recorded, not hidden.

Contamination control. State names and years are stripped from the prompt text where they are not needed, so the model judges the text and not what it remembers about the famous measure.

Cross-model check. A second model family re-codes a sample. Agreement between models is reported next to agreement with the human coder.

docs.title: Retrieval stack
docs.text: Dense embeddings from a legal-domain model (Voyage), with sentence-transformers as a local fallback. rank_bm25 for keyword scoring. Fusion in about twenty lines of Python.

docs.title: What the pipeline does not do
docs.text: It does not decide severity. There is no severity field. It records what changed and in which direction, and the reader judges how much that matters.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: Current version: 0.2. The codebook is the single source of truth. Tests import enums from it.

docs.title: Unit of analysis
docs.text: A provision is a separately survivable unit. An enumerated item is its own provision if the legislature could delete it while leaving its siblings intact and the statute would still be coherent. Otherwise it is a component: it keeps a record, with parent_spine_id set and counts_in_denominator: false. Typography does not decide this; the test is applied by reading the text. See ADR 0001.

docs.title: Spine
docs.text: IDs look like MO-2024-PropA-p017. They are assigned on the base witness (the voter text) and never reassigned. A provision the legislature adds gets its own ID, flagged as having no initiative counterpart. Restructuring is one-to-many. See ADR 0002.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
# Layer Nature Notes 1 Structural operation Near-objective What happened to the text. Assigned by comparing base witness to the amending bill, never to the prior statute 2 Provision type Near-objective What kind of rule it is 3 Directional effect Interpretive Narrows, expands, neutral, indeterminate. Carries a rationale and a driving span 4 Mechanism Interpretive How a narrowing or delay was achieved. Only applies where Layer 3 narrows or delays. Includes escalation removal (added in v0.2) 5 Description and justification Bill-level How the change was described. A binary gap flag 6 Temporal and procedural Near-objective, bill-level Committee of origin, timing, referendum-proof clause 7 Measure context Near-objective Prior and subsequent similar-measure years, stored and not thresholded 8 Subsequent fate Near-objective Includes re-enacted in substantially the same form 9 Coding metadata Who coded it, when, schema version, agreement

There is no severity field. See ADR 0003.

docs.title: Fields added after the prototype (v0.2)
docs.text:
• provenance (created, amended, inherited, uncertain) and provenance_basis
  • depends_on, depended_on_by (the latter derived mechanically by inverting the former)
  • dependency_affected, dependency_source_ids (top level, separate from the exemption sweep)
  • parent_spine_id, counts_in_denominator
  • Layer 4 value escalation removal

docs.title: Denominator rule
docs.text: A record counts toward a survival rate only if counts_in_denominator == true and provenance is created or amended. Inherited and uncertain records stay visible as context. See ADR 0005.

docs.title: Known gaps, proposed for v0.3 and not applied
docs.text:
1. Multi-witness comparison: survival indexed over time, as a provision can differ at each amending bill.
  2. A replaced_by field (South Dakota: a deleted provision was substituted by a different one).
  3. A Layer 1 value for judicial restoration (Michigan).
  4. A policy_pillar field to group provisions by function.

These are batched on purpose. Changing the schema one case at a time makes cases incomparable. All schema changes go through a migration: bump schema_version, update the codebook, the changelog and an ADR.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Status: designed. No pipeline output has been validated yet, because no hand-coded gold exists.

docs.title: Why gold must be hand-coded
docs.text: The prototype file for Missouri Prop A was coded by a model. Every record says so. It is a hypothesis, not ground truth, and it is not used to evaluate the pipeline until a human has audited it. See ADR 0004.

docs.title: Three classes of test
docs.text:
1. Deterministic unit tests. Does the splitter produce the expected provisions? Do IDs stay stable on re-run?
  2. Invariants. Rules that must hold for any correct output, with no gold needed:
    • outright repeal in Layer 4 implies deleted entirely in Layer 1
    • dependency inversion has zero mismatches
    • every component's dependencies appear in its parent's
    • every quoted span matches the source at its stated offsets
  3. Evals. Pipeline output against gold, scored per layer by exact match against closed enums. No LLM judge is needed.

docs.title: Dev and held-out split
docs.text: Gold is split before any prompt is written. The pipeline is tuned on the dev split. The held-out split is run once, after the pipeline is frozen. Without this, the prompts overfit to the cases they were tuned on and the reported agreement is inflated.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text: Pre-registered after the first measurement and before tuning, and written into the repo with a date. Not chosen in advance, because there is no baseline to set them from.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
• Missouri p003 must come out dependency_affected: true.
  • The aligner must return none on the South Dakota IM 22 deletions.

docs.title: Human ceiling
docs.text: A second coder codes a subset. Agreement between two humans is the ceiling the pipeline can reasonably be asked to reach, and is reported beside pipeline agreement.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Agreement is reported per layer, never as one overall number. Interpretive layers (3, 4) will be lower than near-objective ones, and a blended figure would hide that.

docs.title: How we got here
docs.text:
The abandoned directions are recorded because the reasons for abandoning them became the design criteria.

Direction Why it was dropped Model-bill diffusion in state AI legislation A January 2026 ACLU/Brown report covered adjacent ground, and the project moved away from AI as subject matter Ballot title fidelity Sound and novel (existing work measures readability, not accuracy) but tabled. The provision-decomposition machinery carried forward Post-Grants Pass ordinance drafting The advisor objected that a null result (ordinances stay facially neutral) was predictable, and that text is a weak proxy for effects on people Doctrinal migration after Grants Pass Better, but pivoted away from Alteration of initiatives: measurement paper Redirected by the advisor toward a browsable resource, with the Frankenstein Variorum as precedent

docs.title: Design criteria that survived
docs.text:
1. The finding must not be predictable from the armchair.
  2. A null result must still be a finding.
  3. Textual analysis must connect to consequences.
  4. Novelty is checked against existing literature before commitment and claimed narrowly.

docs.title: Borrowed from the Frankenstein Variorum
docs.text: The witness model, the collation spine, heatmap-led navigation, Method and Data as first-class pages, and the dated snapshot. What legal text adds is direction: a deletion narrows and an exemption narrows, where a literary variant has no direction. The visualization therefore needs a second channel for it.

docs.title: The phenomenon
docs.text:
Twenty-one states let citizens enact statutes by initiative. In eleven of them the legislature can amend or repeal an initiated statute by simple majority, immediately. Eight impose time or supermajority limits. Arizona and California require voter approval or purpose-fidelity for substantive change.

Of initiated statutes approved 2010–2018, 28 of 99 had been repealed or amended as of April 2019. Marijuana was the most-altered topic, followed by elections.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: Trackers record that an initiative was altered. They cannot distinguish a legislature implementing a measure from one hollowing it out. No dataset measures how much of a voter-enacted law survives.

docs.title: What this project builds
docs.text:
1. A measurement: provision-level survival, coded in a nine-layer schema that separates what the text did from what the change means.
  2. A method: persistent provision IDs, a hybrid retrieval and LLM-adjudication pipeline, and a validation design built on hand-coded ground truth.
  3. A resource: a browsable, citable, dated-snapshot website over the coded cases.

docs.title: Novelty, stated narrowly
docs.text: Established phenomenon, established method family, measurement nobody has taken. Comparative politics measures textual change with minimum-edit-distance methods. Those score a full rewording as a large change and a nine-word exemption elsewhere as a trivial one, and both readings are wrong. Measuring legal effect requires semantic judgment. This is an application novelty, not a contribution to natural language processing, and it is claimed as nothing more.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• Initiated statutes only.
  • Formal legal change only. Non-enforcement and underfunding are not captured.
  • Small n. Description and typology, not hypothesis testing.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: How the work is done, so that it can be audited and repeated.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Grill. An agent interrogates the plan against the existing docs until the ambiguities are gone. Decisions are written to ADRs and terms to the glossary.
  2. Spec. The settled plan becomes a spec in spec/.
  3. Tickets. The spec is broken into small independent tickets.
  4. Implement. Tickets are built in parallel by subagents, each given the codebook and one case.
  5. Evaluate. Output is scored against gold, and the result is written to the experiment log.
  6. Retro. Friction is logged and feeds the next schema batch.

docs.title: Eval first
docs.text: Gold and the eval spec are written before the pipeline. The evals are the specification: a pipeline stage is done when it passes its evals, not when it looks right.

docs.title: Rules for agents
docs.text: See CLAUDE.md at the repo root. The ones that matter most: agents never write to gold/; quoted spans must match the source character for character; schema changes only by migration.

docs.title: What every run leaves behind
docs.text:
• An experiment entry with hypothesis, setup, result, and what changed as a consequence
  • Friction-log entries as they happen
  • Timing, for hand-coding, so the labour claim is measured
  • A commit

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text: Long sessions end with a written handoff, so a crashed terminal or a new session loses nothing. State lives in the repo, not in the conversation.
